answer.text:
This is the classic **CMOS inverter (NOT gate)**—a complementary push-pull structure consisting of one PMOS pull-up transistor ($M_2$) and one NMOS pull-down transistor ($M_1$).

---

## 1. Component Identification

| Transistor | Type | Terminal Connections | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **$M_1$** | NMOS (n-channel) | Gate $\rightarrow V_{in}$; Source $\rightarrow$ GND; Drain $\rightarrow V_{out}$ | **Pull-down** (discharges $V_{out}$) |
| **$M_2$** | PMOS (p-channel) | Gate $\rightarrow V_{in}$; Source $\rightarrow V_{DD}$; Drain $\rightarrow V_{out}$ | **Pull-up** (charges $V_{out}$) |

*Implicit body connections:* The NMOS body is tied to ground; the PMOS body is tied to $V_{DD}$.

---

## 2. Static (DC) Operation

Because the gates are tied together, both devices see the same $V_{in}$, but their threshold voltages have opposite signs ($V_{thn} > 0$, $V_{thp} < 0$).

### Case A: $V_{in} = 0$ (Logic “0”)
- **$M_1$ (NMOS):** $V_{GS1} = 0 < V_{thn}$ $\Rightarrow$ **cutoff** (open).
- **$M_2$ (PMOS):** $V_{SG2} = V_{DD} - 0 = V_{DD}$; $V_{GS2} = 0 - V_{DD} = -V_{DD} < V_{thp}$ $\Rightarrow$ **on** (linear/saturation).
- **Result:** $V_{out}$ is pulled up to $V_{DD}$ (Logic “1”).
- **Current:** Ideally $I_{DD} = 0$ because $M_1$ is off (no static path).

### Case B: $V_{in} = V_{DD}$ (Logic “1”)
- **$M_1$ (NMOS):** $V_{GS1} = V_{DD} > V_{thn}$ $\Rightarrow$ **on**.
- **$M_2$ (PMOS):** $V_{GS2} = V_{DD} - V_{DD} = 0 > V_{thp}$ $\Rightarrow$ **cutoff** (open).
- **Result:** $V_{out}$ is pulled down to GND (Logic “0”).
- **Current:** Again ideally $I_{DD} = 0$.

### Case C: $V_{in} \approx V_{DD}/2$ (Transition)
Both transistors can be **simultaneously on**, creating a temporary low-resistance path ($M_2$ from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$, $M_1$ from $V_{out}$ to GND). This causes a **crowbar (short-circuit) current** $I_{sc}$ that peaks during switching.

---

## 3. Voltage Transfer Characteristic (VTC)

The inverter has a high-gain transition region around $V_{in} = V_M$ (the switching threshold).

Using long-channel saturation currents at $V_M$:
$$I_{Dn} = \frac{1}{2}k_n(V_M - V_{thn})^2, \qquad I_{Dp} = \frac{1}{2}k_p(V_{DD} - V_M + V_{thp})^2$$

Setting $I_{Dn} = I_{Dp}$ and solving for $V_M$:
$$\boxed{V_M = \frac{V_{thn} + r(V_{DD} + V_{thp})}{1+r}}$$
where $r = \sqrt{k_n/k_p}$ and $k = \mu C_{ox}(W/L)$.

**Symmetry condition ($V_M = V_{DD}/2$):** If $V_{thn} = |V_{thp}| = V_{th}$, this requires:
$$k_n = k_p \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{(W/L)_p}{(W/L)_n} = \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} \approx 2\text{--}3$$
Because electron mobility $\mu_n \approx 2\!-\!3\times$ hole mobility $\mu_p$, the PMOS is usually sized wider.

**Small-signal gain** in the transition region:
$$A_v = -\frac{g_{mn} + g_{mp}}{g_{dsn} + g_{dsp}} \;\;(\text{large negative value})$$

---

## 4. Dynamic (Transient) Behavior

The output drives a load capacitance $C_L$ (interconnect + next-stage gates).

| Transition | Dominant Device | Charging/Discharging Path | Delay |
|---|---|---|---|
| $V_{in}: 0 \to V_{DD}$ | $M_1$ on, $M_2$ off | $C_L$ discharges through $M_1$ to GND | $t_{PHL}$ |
| $V_{in}: V_{DD} \to 0$ | $M_2$ on, $M_1$ off | $C_L$ charges through $M_2$ to $V_{DD}$ | $t_{PLH}$ |

Approximate expressions (simple RC model):
$$t_{PHL} \approx 0.69 \, R_{on,n} \, C_L, \qquad t_{PLH} \approx 0.69 \, R_{on,p} \, C_L$$

To make $t_{PHL} \approx t_{PLH}$, match on-resistances: $R_{on,p} \approx R_{on,n}$, again requiring $(W/L)_p > (W/L)_n$.

---

## 5. Power Consumption

$$P = P_{static} + P_{dynamic} + P_{sc}$$

- **Static:** $\approx 0$ (no DC path between rails when settled).
- **Dynamic (switching):** $P_{dyn} = C_L V_{DD}^2 f$ (dominant).
- **Short-circuit:** $P_{sc} \approx I_{sc,avg} V_{DD}$ (brief pulse during transitions; minimized by fast input edges).

---

## 6. Key Design / Performance Metrics

| Parameter | Expression / Note |
|---|---|
| **Noise Margin High ($NM_H$)** | $V_{OH} - V_{IH}$; ideally $\approx V_{DD}/2$ |
| **Noise Margin Low ($NM_L$)** | $V_{OL} - V_{IL}$; ideally $\approx V_{DD}/2$ |
| **Output High / Low** | $V_{OH} \approx V_{DD}$, $V_{OL} \approx 0$ |
| **Logic Function** | $V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}$ |

---

## Summary

This circuit is the **fundamental CMOS inverter**. Its complementary nature guarantees:
1. **Full rail-to-rail output swing** ($0$ or $V_{DD}$).
2. **Zero static power dissipation** (ideally).
3. **High noise immunity** due to steep VTC.
4. **Fast switching** governed by transistor drive strengths and load capacitance.

The main design trade-off is transistor sizing: the PMOS is usually made **2–3× wider** than the NMOS to compensate for lower hole mobility and to center the switching threshold at $V_{DD}/2$ for symmetrical delays.

The figure is the classic **CMOS inverter** (also called a complementary MOS NOT gate / push‑pull common‑source amplifier).  
It consists of:

| Transistor | Type | Source | Drain | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M₁** | NMOS (pull‑down) | Ground | $V_{\rm out}$ | $V_{\rm in}$ |
| **M₂** | PMOS (pull‑up) | $V_{\rm DD}$ | $V_{\rm out}$ | $V_{\rm in}$ |

The two gates are driven by the same input; the two drains are shorted to produce the output.

Below is a complete analysis covering DC transfer characteristics, operating regions, small‑signal (analog) gain, and digital performance metrics.

---

## 1. DC Transfer Characteristic ($V_{\rm out}$ vs. $V_{\rm in}$)

### Extreme states
* **$V_{\rm in}=0$ (low)**  
  $V_{GS1}=0<V_{tn}$ → $M_1$ **OFF**.  
  $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{tp}|$ → $M_2$ **ON** (deep triode, $V_{SD2}\approx 0$).  
  No current can flow to ground, so $\boxed{V_{\rm OH}=V_{DD}}$.

* **$V_{\rm in}=V_{DD}$ (high)**  
  $V_{SG2}=0<|V_{tp}|$ → $M_2$ **OFF**.  
  $V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{tn}$ → $M_1$ **ON** (deep triode, $V_{DS1}\approx 0$).  
  $\boxed{V_{\rm OL}=0}$.

Because one device is always off (in steady state), the **static power dissipation is essentially zero**—a key advantage of CMOS.

### Intermediate region & switching threshold $V_M$
As $V_{\rm in}$ rises, both transistors can be on simultaneously. The output is set by balancing the drain currents:
$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$$

Using the long‑channel saturation model ($\lambda=0$ for simplicity):
$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_M-V_{tn})^2=\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^2$$

where $\beta_n=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1$, $\beta_p=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2$, $V_{tn}>0$, and $V_{tp}<0$.

Taking square roots and solving gives the **switching threshold**:
$$\boxed{V_M=\frac{\sqrt{\beta_n}\,V_{tn}+\sqrt{\beta_p}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)}{\sqrt{\beta_n}+\sqrt{\beta_p}}}$$

If the inverter is **symmetrically sized** so that $\beta_n=\beta_p$ (i.e. $(W/L)_p = \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}(W/L)_1$), then:
$$\boxed{V_M=\frac{V_{DD}+V_{tn}-|V_{tp}|}{2}\approx \frac{V_{DD}}{2}}$$

### Five operating regions
As $V_{\rm in}$ increases from 0 to $V_{DD}$:

| Region | $V_{\rm in}$ range | $M_1$ (NMOS) | $M_2$ (PMOS) | $V_{\rm out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | $<V_{tn}$ | Cut‑off | Triode (ON) | $V_{DD}$ |
| II | $V_{tn}\le V_{\rm in}<V_M$ | Saturation | Triode | High, falling |
| III | $\approx V_M$ | **Saturation** | **Saturation** | **Steep drop (high gain)** |
| IV | $V_M< V_{\rm in}\le V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$ | Triode | Saturation | Low, falling |
| V | $>V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$ | Triode (ON) | Cut‑off | $0$ |

Region III is the “high‑gain” analog region.

---

## 2. Small‑Signal (AC) Analysis

Bias the inverter at $V_M$ so both devices are saturated. The small‑signal model is two common‑source devices with sources at AC ground ($M_1$→GND, $M_2$→$V_{DD}$) and gates driven by $v_{\rm in}$.

**Transconductances:**
$$g_{m1}=\sqrt{2\beta_n I_D},\qquad g_{m2}=\sqrt{2\beta_p I_D}$$

**Output resistances (with $\lambda\neq 0$):**
$$r_{o1}=\frac{1}{\lambda_n I_D},\qquad r_{o2}=\frac{1}{\lambda_p I_D}$$

Because $v_{\rm in}$ increasing turns $M_1$ **on harder** (pulls $v_{\rm out}$ down) and turns $M_2$ **weaker** (pulls up less), **both effects reinforce each other**.

Nodal analysis at $v_{\rm out}$ yields:
$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_{\rm in}}=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})}$$

For the symmetric case ($g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$, $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o$):
$$A_v=-g_m\left(\frac{r_o}{2}\right)=-g_m r_o/2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \boxed{A_v\approx -\frac{2}{\lambda\,(V_{DD}/2-V_{tn})}}$$

* **Input resistance:** $\infty$ (MOS gates are insulated).
* **Output resistance:** $R_{\rm out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$.

Thus, when biased at $V_M$, the CMOS inverter acts as a **high‑gain analog amplifier** (often used as a gain stage or as a comparator/inverter in analog circuits).

---

## 3. Digital Metrics & Performance

| Parameter | Expression / Value |
|---|---|
| **Logic high** | $V_{\rm OH}\approx V_{DD}$ |
| **Logic low** | $V_{\rm OL}\approx 0$ |
| **Noise margin high** | $NM_H = V_{\rm OH}-V_{\rm IH}$ |

|---|---|---|---|

\[

\]

When \(V_{in}\) is low, \(M_2\) pulls the output up to \(V_{DD}\). When \(V_{in}\) is high, \(M_1\) pulls it down to ground.

For intermediate input voltages, approximately

\[

\]

both transistors can conduct. A direct current then flows from \(V_{DD}\) to ground, and the output moves rapidly between its two logic levels.

2. **\(M_1\) saturation, \(M_2\) triode:** output begins to fall.
3. **Both transistors saturated:** output resistance is high and the transfer characteristic is very steep.
4. **\(M_1\) triode, \(M_2\) saturation:** output approaches ground.
5. **\(M_1\) triode, \(M_2\) cutoff:** output remains at zero.

The small-signal voltage gain near the middle of the transition is approximately

\[
\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
\approx-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})}
\]

so the circuit can also be viewed as a high-gain inverting amplifier when biased in this region.

\[
V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M.

\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_M-V_{TN})^2

{\sqrt{\beta_n}+\sqrt{\beta_p}}
}
\]

\[

# CMOS Inverter Analysis

The circuit shown is a **complementary MOS (CMOS) inverter**, the fundamental building block of modern digital logic.

## 1. Circuit Topology

- **M₁**: NMOS transistor → acts as a **pull-down** network (connects output to ground)
- **M₂**: PMOS transistor → acts as a **pull-up** network (connects output to VDD)
- Both gates are tied to the input $V_{in}$
- The output $V_{out}$ is taken from the common drain node

## 2. DC Operation / Truth Table

| $V_{in}$ | M₁ (NMOS) | M₂ (PMOS) | $V_{out}$ | State |
|----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| 0 (LOW)  | OFF       | ON        | $V_{DD}$  | Logic HIGH |
| $V_{DD}$ (HIGH) | ON  | OFF       | 0         | Logic LOW |

Key observation: In either steady state, **one transistor is always OFF**, so there is ideally no static current path from $V_{DD}$ to ground.

## 3. Voltage Transfer Characteristic (VTC)

The VTC can be divided into five regions:

1. **$0 \leq V_{in} < V_{THN}$** → M₁ OFF, M₂ ON (linear) → $V_{out} = V_{DD}$
2. **$V_{THN} \leq V_{in} < V_M$** → M₁ ON (saturation), M₂ ON (linear) → $V_{out}$ begins falling
3. **$V_{in} \approx V_M$** → Both M₁ and M₂ in saturation → steep transition, maximum voltage gain
4. **$V_M < V_{in} \leq V_{DD} - |V_{THP}|$** → M₁ ON (linear), M₂ ON (saturation) → $V_{out}$ approaches 0
5. **$V_{DD} - |V_{THP}| < V_{in} \leq V_{DD}$** → M₁ ON (linear), M₂ OFF → $V_{out} = 0$

## 4. Switching Threshold $V_M$

The switching threshold is the point where $V_{in} = V_{out}$. At this point, both transistors are saturated. Equating drain currents:

$$I_{D1} = I_{D2}$$

$$\frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_M - V_{THN})^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_{DD} - V_M - |V_{THP}|)^2$$

Solving:

$$V_M = \frac{\sqrt{k_n}V_{THN} + \sqrt{k_p}(V_{DD} - |V_{THP}|)}{\sqrt{k_n} + \sqrt{k_p}}$$

where $k_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1$ and $k_p = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_2$.

For a **symmetric inverter** with $k_n = k_p$ and $V_{THN} = |V_{THP}|$:

$$\boxed{V_M = \frac{V_{DD}}{2}}$$

## 5. Noise Margins

Noise margins quantify how much noise the circuit can tolerate:

$$NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}$$
$$NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}$$

For an ideal CMOS inverter:
- $V_{OH} \approx V_{DD}$
- $V_{OL} \approx 0$
- The transition region is very steep (high small-signal gain)

This gives CMOS inverters **excellent noise margins** and high noise immunity.

## 6. Power Consumption

- **Static power**: Ideally zero (no direct $V_{DD}$-to-ground path in steady state)
- **Dynamic power**: Dominates at high frequencies
  $$P_{dyn} = C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$
  where $C_L$ is load capacitance and $f$ is switching frequency
- **Short-circuit power**: Small power dissipated during transitions when both transistors briefly conduct
- **Leakage power**: Subthreshold and gate leakage in modern technologies

## 7. Propagation Delay

- $t_{PHL}$: determined by NMOS current discharging $C_L$
- $t_{PLH}$: determined by PMOS current charging $C_L$

For symmetric sizing, the rise and fall delays are approximately equal.

## Summary

The CMOS inverter is valued for:
- Full rail-to-rail output swing (0 to $V_{DD}$)
- Negligible static power dissipation
- Large noise margins
- High input impedance
- Regenerative logic levels

It is the cornerstone of CMOS digital integrated circuits.

The circuit is a **CMOS inverter**, the most fundamental building block in digital CMOS logic.

- \(M_1\) is an **NMOS** transistor with its source grounded.
- \(M_2\) is a **PMOS** transistor with its source tied to \(V_{DD}\).
- The gates of both transistors are connected together to the input \(V_{in}\).
- The drains of both transistors are connected together to form the output \(V_{out}\).

---

## 1. Basic DC Operation

The inverter has two stable states:

| Input \(V_{in}\) | NMOS \(M_1\) | PMOS \(M_2\) | Output \(V_{out}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low** (\(\approx 0\)) | OFF | ON | **High** (\(\approx V_{DD}\)) |
| **High** (\(\approx V_{DD}\)) | ON | OFF | **Low** (\(\approx 0\)) |

- When \(V_{in}\) is low, the NMOS is off and the PMOS pulls the output up to \(V_{DD}\).
- When \(V_{in}\) is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS pulls the output down to ground.

Thus, the logic function is:

\[
V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}
\]

---

## 2. Voltage Transfer Characteristic (VTC)

As \(V_{in}\) sweeps from \(0\) to \(V_{DD}\), the output transitions from \(V_{DD}\) to \(0\). The VTC has three key regions:

1. **Region I:** \(V_{in} < V_{thn}\)  
   - NMOS is off, PMOS is on (triode/linear).  
   - \(V_{out} \approx V_{DD}\).

2. **Region II:** Around the switching point  
   - Both transistors are on and operate in saturation.  
   - The output changes rapidly with high gain.

3. **Region III:** \(V_{in} > V_{DD} - |V_{thp}|\)  
   - PMOS is off, NMOS is on (triode/linear).  
   - \(V_{out} \approx 0\).

The **switching threshold** \(V_M\) is the point where \(V_{in} = V_{out}\). Assuming both transistors are in saturation:

\[
\frac{1}{2}k_n(V_M - V_{thn})^2 = \frac{1}{2}k_p(V_{DD} - V_M - |V_{thp}|)^2
\]

where \(k = \mu C_{ox}(W/L)\). Solving gives:

\[
V_M = \frac{V_{thn} + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}(V_{DD} - |V_{thp}|)}
{1 + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}}
\]

For perfectly symmetric devices (\(V_{thn} = |V_{thp}|\), \(k_n = k_p\)):

\[
\boxed{V_M = \frac{V_{DD}}{2}}
\]

This gives equal and maximum noise margins for both logic levels.

---

## 3. Noise Margins

The noise margins measure how much unwanted voltage the gate can tolerate without producing an incorrect logic value.

\[
NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}
\]

\[
NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}
\]

For an ideal symmetric CMOS inverter:

\[
NM_H \approx NM_L \approx \frac{V_{DD}}{2}
\]

This makes CMOS very robust against noise and interference.

---

## 4. Small-Signal Gain

Around the switching threshold, both transistors conduct, and the inverter behaves like a high-gain inverting amplifier.

The small-signal voltage gain is:

\[
A_v \approx -(g_{mn} + g_{mp})(r_{on} \parallel r_{op})
\]

where:
- \(g_{mn}, g_{mp}\) are the transconductances of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\),
- \(r_{on}, r_{op}\) are their output resistances.

The gain is large in the transition region, which is what gives the inverter its sharp switching behavior.

---

## 5. Dynamic Behavior

When the input changes, the output does not change instantly because it must charge or discharge the load capacitance \(C_L\), which includes:

- gate/drain overlap capacitances,
- drain-bulk junction capacitances,
- interconnect capacitance,
- input capacitance of the next stage.

The propagation delay is approximately:

\[
t_p \approx \frac{C_L V_{DD}}{2 I_{drive}}
\]

where \(I_{drive}\) is the average current of the charging/discharging transistor.

---

## 6. Power Consumption

A major advantage of CMOS is its low static power:

\[
P_{static} \approx 0
\]

because at steady state, one transistor is always off, blocking the path from \(V_{DD}\) to ground.

However, dynamic power is dissipated when the output switches:

\[
P_{dynamic} = C_L V_{DD}^2 f
\]

where:
- \(C_L\) is the load capacitance,
- \(f\) is the switching frequency.

There is also a small **short-circuit power** during the brief time both transistors are on while the input transitions.

---

## 7. Summary

| Feature | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Logic function** | Inverter: \(V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}\) |
| **Output swing** | Rail-to-rail: \(0\) to \(V_{DD}\) |
| **Static power** | Approximately zero |
| **Noise margin** | High, ideally near \(V_{DD}/2\) |
| **Gain** | High around switching point |
| **Speed** | Limited by load capacitance and drive current |

Therefore, the circuit functions as a **low-power, high-noise-margin digital inverter**, and is the cornerstone of modern CMOS digital systems.

\[

\[
\beta_n=\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_1,\qquad
\beta_p=\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_2
\]

\[

\begin{cases}
0, & V_{in}\le V_{TN}\\[2mm]
\beta_n\left[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\dfrac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right],
& V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{TN}\\[3mm]

\end{cases}
\]

For the pMOS \(M_2\):

\[
I_{D2}=
\begin{cases}
0, & V_{in}\ge V_{DD}-V_{tp}\\[2mm]
\beta_p\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{tp})(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\dfrac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\right],
& V_{out}>V_{in}+V_{tp}\\[3mm]
\dfrac{\beta_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{tp})^2,
& V_{out}\le V_{in}+V_{tp}
\end{cases}
\]

\[
\boxed{I_{D1}=I_{D2}}
\]

\[

\[
\boxed{V_{out}=0}
\]

Ideally there is no static current in either logic state.

\[

=
\sqrt{\beta_p}\,(V_{DD}-V_M-V_{tp})
\]

so

\[

V_M=
\frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\,(V_{DD}-V_{tp})}
{1+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}}
}
\]

If \(\beta_n=\beta_p\) and \(V_{TN}=V_{tp}\), then

\[
\boxed{V_M=\frac{V_{DD}}{2}}
\]

\]

often about 2–3 times wider for the pMOS.

\[

## 1. Logic operation

| $V_{in}$ | $M_1$ (nMOS) | $M_2$ (pMOS) | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low ($<V_{THN}$) | OFF | ON (triode, $I_D=0$) | $V_{DD}$ = logic 1 |
| High ($>V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$) | ON (triode, $I_D=0$) | OFF | $0$ = logic 0 |

So $V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$, with **rail‑to‑rail output swing**. In either static logic state one transistor is cut off, so there is no dc path from $V_{DD}$ to ground and the **static (quiescent) power is ideally zero** (only leakage in practice).

## 2. Voltage‑transfer characteristic (five regions)

| Region | Condition | $M_1$ | $M_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $V_{in}<V_{THN}$ | cutoff | triode ($V_{out}=V_{DD}$) |
| 2 | $V_{in}>V_{THN}$, $V_{out}>V_{in}+|V_{THP}|$ | saturation | triode |
| 3 | $V_{in}-V_{THN}<V_{out}<V_{in}+|V_{THP}|$ | saturation | saturation |
| 4 | $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{THN}$ | triode | saturation |
| 5 | $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$ | triode ($V_{out}=0$) | cutoff |

In region 3 both devices are saturated; equating currents (neglecting channel‑length modulation) gives the **switching threshold** $V_M$:

$$
\sqrt{\beta_n}\,(V_M-V_{THN})=\sqrt{\beta_p}\,(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|)
$$

$$
\boxed{\;V_M=\frac{V_{THN}+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|)}{1+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}}\;}
$$

For a **matched** inverter ($\beta_n=\beta_p$, $V_{THN}=|V_{THP}|$), $V_M=V_{DD}/2$. Ideally ( $\lambda=0$ ) the transition at $V_M$ is vertical; with finite output resistance the small‑signal gain there is

$$
A_v=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}),
$$

which reduces to $|A_v|=g_m r_o$ for the symmetric case.

For the matched design the unity‑slope points are

$$
V_{IL}=\frac{3V_{DD}+2V_{TH}}{8},\qquad 
V_{IH}=\frac{5V_{DD}-2V_{TH}}{8},
$$

so $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$ and $NM_H=NM_L$.

## 3. Current and power

- **Short‑circuit (crowbar) current:** while $V_{THN}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$ both transistors conduct. It peaks near $V_M$:
$$
I_{SC,pk}\approx \tfrac12\beta\!\left(\tfrac{V_{DD}}{2}-V_{TH}\right)^{2}
$$
(matched case).
- **Dynamic power** into a load $C_L$ at frequency $f$ with activity factor $\alpha$:
$$
P_{dyn}=\alpha\, C_L V_{DD}^{2} f ,
$$
plus a smaller short‑circuit power term during the input transition.

## 4. Design note

Because $\mu_n>\mu_p$, equal rise and fall times ($t_{PHL}$ set by $M_1$, $t_{PLH}$ by $M_2$) require

$$
\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}=\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}\approx 2\text{–}3 ,
$$

i.e. the pMOS is made wider than the nMOS. Sizing for $\beta_n=\beta_p$ also centers $V_M$ at $V_{DD}/2$ and maximizes the (symmetric) noise margins.

This is a **CMOS Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Inverter, a basic NOT logic gate**, the foundational circuit for all CMOS digital logic. Let's break down its operation and characteristics:

1.  **Device Identification**:
    -   $M_1$ is an **nMOS NMOS Transistor**: Source tied to ground, drain tied to $V_{out}$, gate tied to $V_{in}$.
    -   $M_2$ is a **pMOS PMOS Transistor**: Source tied to $V_{DD}$, drain tied to $V_{out}$, gate tied to $V_{in}$, sharing the input connection with $M_1$.

2.  **Operation based on Input $V_{in}$**:
    -   **Case 1: $V_{in} \approx V_{DD}$ (High Input)**
        -   $M_1$ nMOS: $V_{GS} = V_{in} - 0 = V_{DD} > V_{tn}$ (nMOS threshold voltage), so $M_1$ **conducts, turns ON**, pulling $V_{out}$ down to ground, $\approx 0$.
        -   $M_2$ pMOS: $V_{SG} = V_{DD} - V_{in} \approx 0 < |V_{tp}|$ (pMOS threshold voltage), so $M_2$ **turns OFF**.
        -   Result: $V_{out} \approx 0$, Logic **LOW** output.

    -   **Case 2: $V_{in} \approx 0$ (Low Input)**
        -   $M_1$ nMOS: $V_{GS} = 0 - 0 = 0 < V_{tn}$, so $M_1$ **turns OFF**.
        -   $M_2$ pMOS: $V_{SG} = V_{DD} - 0 = V_{DD} > |V_{tp}|$, so $M_2$ **conducts, turns ON**, pulling $V_{out}$ up to $V_{DD}$.
        -   Result: $V_{out} \approx V_{DD}$, Logic **HIGH** output.

3.  **Key Characteristics**:

- **M₁ (NMOS)**: Source connected to ground, drain to V_out

| V_in | M₁ (NMOS) | M₂ (PMOS) | V_out |
|------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| LOW (0) | OFF | ON | HIGH (≈ V_DD) |
| HIGH (V_DD) | ON | OFF | LOW (≈ 0) |

### When V_in = LOW (Logic 0):
- V_GS1 ≈ 0 → M₁ is **off** (no path from V_out to GND)
- V_GS2 = −V_DD → M₂ is **on** (pulls V_out up to V_DD)
- **Output = V_DD (Logic 1)**

### When V_in = HIGH (Logic 1):
- V_GS1 = V_DD → M₁ is **on** (pulls V_out down to GND)
- V_GS2 ≈ 0 → M₂ is **off** (no path from V_out to V_DD)
- **Output = 0 (Logic 0)**

## Key Properties

1. **Logic inversion**: Implements the Boolean NOT function (V_out = ¬V_in)

2. **Rail-to-rail swing**: Output swings from 0 to V_DD in steady state (ideal noise margins).

3. **Static power dissipation is essentially zero**: In either steady state, one transistor is OFF, so no direct DC current flows from V_DD to ground.

4. **Dynamic power**: Power is dissipated only during switching when both transistors conduct briefly, charging/discharging the load capacitance:
$$P_{dyn} = \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$
where α is the switching activity factor.

5. **High input impedance**: The gate is insulated (MOS structure), so the input draws negligible DC current.

6. **Low output impedance (in active region)**: During transitions, the transistors provide low-resistance paths to either rail, enabling fast switching of capacitive loads.

## Transfer Characteristic (VTC)

The VTC is symmetric when W₂/L₂ is sized appropriately (typically 2–3× W₁/L₁) to compensate for the lower mobility of holes versus electrons. The switching threshold V_M is set by the ratio of transconductances:
$$V_M = \frac{V_{TH,n} + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}(V_{DD} - |V_{TH,p}|)}{1 + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}}$$

This inverter is used as a standalone logic gate, as a buffer, and as the basic cell replicated thousands of times in static CMOS logic gates (NAND, NOR, etc.).

# CMOS Inverter Circuit Analysis

## Circuit Identification

This is a **CMOS Inverter** (NOT gate), consisting of:
- **M₂**: PMOS transistor (top) — source connected to V_DD
- **M₁**: NMOS transistor (bottom) — source connected to ground
- **V_in**: Common gate input to both transistors
- **V_out**: Common drain output of both transistors

## Operating Principle

The two MOSFETs operate in **complementary fashion** — when one is ON, the other is OFF:

| State | V_in | M₁ (NMOS) | M₂ (PMOS) | V_out |
|-------|------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| **Input LOW** | 0 V | OFF (V_GS = 0) | ON (V_SG = V_DD) | **V_DD** (HIGH) |
| **Input HIGH** | V_DD | ON (V_GS = V_DD) | OFF (V_SG = 0) | **0 V** (LOW) |

### Logic Equation:
$$V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}$$

## Transfer Characteristics

```
V_out
  V_DD ──────────────────────╲
                              ╲
                              ╲  ← Transition region
                               ╲   (both transistors ON)
                                ╲
   0 ─────────────────────────────╲───── V_in
   0    V_TN          V_M        V_DD-|V_TP|   V_DD
```

The **switching threshold** (V_M), where V_in = V_out, is typically designed near V_DD/2 by proper sizing of the transistors:

$$V_M \approx \frac{V_{TN} + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}\,(V_{DD} - |V_{TP}|)}{1 + \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}}}$$

## Key Advantages

| Feature | Benefit |
|---------|---------|
| **Rail-to-rail output swing** | Full noise margins (0 to V_DD) |
| **Zero static current** | Only one transistor is ON at a time → no DC path from V_DD to GND |
| **Low static power** | P_static ≈ 0 |
| **High input impedance** | No DC loading on driving circuit |
| **Symmetric drive** | Both high-to-low and low-to-low transitions available |

## Power Consumption

The dynamic power dissipation dominates:

$$P_{dynamic} = C_L \cdot V_{DD}^2 \cdot f_{sw}$$

Where:
- $C_L$ = load capacitance at the output
- $f_{sw}$ = switching frequency

## Summary

This CMOS inverter is the **fundamental building block** of all digital CMOS logic. Its complementary pull-up (PMOS) and pull-down (NMOS) network ensures that:
- Output is actively driven **HIGH** or **LOW** (not weakly held)
- Power is consumed **only during transitions**
- Logic inversion is achieved with maximum noise immunity

More complex gates (NAND, NOR, XOR, flip-flops, etc.) are constructed by combining multiple such inverter-like structures with series/parallel transistor arrangements.

---

The circuit acts as a logical inverter:

| Input State ($V_{\text{in}}$) | $M_1$ (NMOS) State | $M_2$ (PMOS) State | Output State ($V_{\text{out}}$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **LOW** ($0\text{ V}$, Logic '0') | OFF (Cut-off) | ON (Triode/Linear) | **HIGH** ($V_{DD}$, Logic '1') |
| **HIGH** ($V_{DD}$, Logic '1') | ON (Triode/Linear) | OFF (Cut-off) | **LOW** ($0\text{ V}$, Logic '0') |

* **When $V_{\text{in}} = 0\text{ V}$:** 
  * $V_{GS1} = 0 < V_{THN}$ $\rightarrow$ $M_1$ is **OFF**.
  * $V_{GS2} = -V_{DD}$, and since $|V_{GS2}| > |V_{THP}|$ $\rightarrow$ $M_2$ is **ON**, acting as a closed switch connecting $V_{\text{out}}$ directly to $V_{DD}$.
* **When $V_{\text{in}} = V_{DD}$:**

1. **Region A ($V_{\text{in}} < V_{THN}$):** $M_1$ is OFF, $M_2$ is in the **triode region**. $V_{\text{out}} \approx V_{DD}$.
2. **Region B ($V_{THN} \le V_{\text{in}} < V_M$):** $M_1$ enters **saturation**, $M_2$ remains in the **triode region**. $V_{\text{out}}$ begins to drop.

* **Output:** $V_{\text{out}}$ is connected directly to $V_{DD}$ and isolated from ground. Therefore, **$V_{\text{out}} = \text{HIGH}$ (Logic 1, } \approx V_{DD}$)**.

* **$M_2$ (PMOS):** $V_{SG2} = V_{DD} - V_{\text{in}} = 0\text{ V} < |V_{TP}|$, so $M_2$ is in **cutoff (OFF)**.

1. **Region 1 ($V_{\text{in}} < V_{TN}$):** $M_1$ is OFF, $M_2$ is in deep triode. $V_{\text{out}} = V_{DD}$.
2. **Region 2 ($V_{TN} < V_{\text{in}} < V_{DD} - |V_{TP}|$):** $M_1$ enters saturation, $M_2$ remains in triode. $V_{\text{out}}$ starts to decrease.
3. **Region 3 (Switching Region, $V_{\text{in}} \approx V_M$):** Both $M_1$ and $M_2$ are in **saturation**. In this narrow region, a tiny change in $V_{\text{in}}$ causes a massive change in $V_{\text{out}}$ (very high gain, ideally infinite).

| **Parameter**               | **Description**                                                                 |

  - **Near zero** in stable states (no DC path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground).  
  - Only **leakage currents** (subthreshold, gate oxide) contribute, which are negligible in modern CMOS.  
- **Dynamic Power (P<sub>dynamic</sub>)**:  
  Dominated by **switching losses**:  
  $$
  P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha \cdot C_L \cdot V_{DD}^2 \cdot f
  $$  
  where:  
  - **α** = Activity factor (fraction of time the circuit switches),  
  - **C<sub>L</sub>** = Load capacitance,  
  - **f** = Operating frequency.  

#### **(c) Transistor Operating Regions**
| **Input (V<sub>in</sub>)** | **M₂ (PMOS)** | **M₁ (NMOS)** |
|----------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| **V<sub>in</sub> = 0 V**   | **Triode** (V<sub>DS</sub> = 0) | **Cutoff** |
| **V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/2** | **Saturation** | **Saturation** |
| **V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>** | **Cutoff** | **Triode** (V<sub>DS</sub> = 0) |

- **Triode Region**: Occurs when **V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>GS</sub> – |V<sub>th</sub>|** (for PMOS) or **V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>GS</sub> – V<sub>th</sub>** (for NMOS).  
- **Saturation Region**: Occurs when **V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> – |V<sub>th</sub>|** (PMOS) or **V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> – V<sub>th</sub>** (NMOS).

---

---

### **4. Advantages of CMOS Inverter**
1. **Full-Rail Output**: **V<sub>out</sub>** swings from **0 V to V<sub>DD</sub>**, maximizing noise immunity.  
2. **Low Static Power**: Ideal for battery-powered devices.  
3. **High Input Impedance**: Gates of MOSFETs draw negligible current.  
4. **Scalability**: Works across a wide range of supply voltages (from sub-1V to several volts).  
5. **Complementary Operation**: Only one transistor conducts in static states, minimizing leakage.

---
---
### **5. Summary**
The circuit is a **CMOS inverter**, which:
- **Inverts** the input signal (**V<sub>out</sub> = ¬V<sub>in</sub>**).  
- Operates with **near-zero static power** due to complementary transistor action.  
- Has a **sharp voltage transfer characteristic** with a switching threshold at **~V<sub>DD</sub>/2**.  
- Exhibits **high noise margins** and **full-rail output swing**.  
- Is the **cornerstone of CMOS digital logic**, used in all modern microprocessors and ICs.

For deeper analysis, one could derive the **VTC equation**, calculate **propagation delay**, or optimize transistor sizing for speed/power trade-offs. However, the core functionality and advantages are as described above.

The circuit is the **Complementary MOS In - NOT - {\it Inverter}**. 
It is the basic ${\it ratioless}$ static CMOS logic
gate. $M_{1}= n-MOS$ , $M_{2}= p-MOS$, enhancement mode.

$$S_{1}= {\rm GND}, B_{1}= {\rm GND} \;\;,\;\; S_{2}= V_{DD}, B_{2}=V_{DD}$$

so source-body junctions always reverse biased. 
Gates common $=V_{in}$ , Drains common $=V_{out}$ - push - pull
common source with active load.

In digital terms:

$$V_{out}= \bar V_{in}$$

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ nMOS | $M_{2}$ pMOS | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0 = GND =``0"$ | $V_{GS1}=0<V_{Tn}$ {\it OFF} | $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{Tp}|$ {\it ON} lin. | $V_{DD}=``1"$ |
| $V_{DD}=``1"$ | $V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{Tn}$ {\it ON} lin. | $V_{SG2}=0<|V_{Tp}|$ {\it OFF} | $0=``0"$ |

No DC path $V_{DD}\to GND$ in either stable logic state. Static current $I_{DD}=0$ except leakage and during transition. High input impedance $\approx \infty$, rail to rail output swing, large noise margin.

### 1. DC Transfer Characteristic $V_{out}=f(V_{in})$ $0\le V_{in}\le V_{DD}$

With $I_{Dn}= -I_{Dp}$ current:

* nMOS: $I_{Dn}=0$ if $V_{GS}<V_{Tn}$, $k_{n}(V_{GS}-V_{Tn})^{2}/2$ in saturation, $k_{n}[2(V_{GS}-V_{Tn})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^{2}]/2$ in triode.

* pMOS: $I_{Dp}=0$ if $V_{SG}<|V_{Tp}|$, analogous with $V_{SG}, V_{SD}$

where $k_{n,p}= \mu_{n,p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{n,p}= \beta_{n,p}$

$$V_{Tn}>0 \;\;,\;\; V_{Tp}<0$$

In the sweep $V_{in}:0\to V_{DD}$ 5 regions:

1.  $0\le V_{in}<V_{Tn}$ : $M_{1}$ cut-off, $M_{2}$ triode
    $$I_{D}=0,\; V_{out}=V_{DD}=V_{OH}$$

2.  $V_{Tn}<V_{in}< V_{IL}$ : $M_{1}$ saturation, $M_{2}$ triode

3.  $V_{IL}<V_{in}<V_{IH}$ : **both saturation** - high gain transition. $I_{D}$ maximum. 
    The logic threshold $V_{M}$ defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}$ and $I_{Dn}=-I_{Dp}$ in saturation:
    $$\frac{k_{n}}{2}(V_{M}-V_{Tn})^{2}= \frac{k_{p}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{M}+V_{Tp})^{2}$$
    $$V_{M}= \frac{V_{Tn}+ \sqrt{k_{p}/k_{n}}\,(V_{DD}+V_{Tp})}{1+\sqrt{k_{p}/k_{n}}}$$
    For symmetric inverter $V_{Tn}=|V_{Tp}|=V_{T}$ and matched $\beta$ ,
    $$V_{M}\approx V_{DD}/2$$
    Condition for $V_{M}=V_{DD}/2$:
    $$\frac{(W/L)_{p}}{(W/L)_{n}} = \frac{\mu_{n}}{\mu_{p}}\approx 2-3$$

4.  $V_{IH}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$ : $M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ saturation

5.  $V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|<V_{in}\le V_{DD}$ : $M_{2}$ cut-off, $M_{1}$ triode
    $$I_{D}=0,\; V_{out}=0=V_{OL}$$

This gives the familiar sharp, inverting VTC with three points $V_{IL},V_{M},V_{IH}$ defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$.

$$V_{OH}=V_{DD},\;V_{OL}=0$$
$$NM_{L}=V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{M},\; NM_{H}=V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{M}$$
Ideal $\approx V_{DD}/2$ - maximum noise immunity.

> In current domain $I_{DD}(V_{in})$ is $\approx 0$ in regions 1,5 and is a narrow peaked pulse $\approx k(V_{M}-V_{T})^{2}/2$ in region 3 - the short circuit current during switching.

### 2. Small signal - Analog amplifier

Biased at $V_{in}=V_{M}$, both in saturation:

$$A_{v}= \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} = -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}||r_{o2})$$

Typical $|A_{v}| \approx 10-100$, inverting common source. $g_{m}=k(V_{GS}-V_{T})$, $r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}$. Used as high gain inverting stage, crystal oscillator, etc.

Input capacitance $C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd1}+C_{gd2}$ Miller, output resistance $r_{o1}||r_{o2}$.

### 3. Dynamic - Transient

Capacitive load $C_{L}$ at $V_{out}$.

* Pull-up through $M_{2}$ : $t_{pLH}\approx 0.69\,R_{p}C_{L}$
* Pull-down through $M_{1}$ : $t_{pHL}\approx 0.69\,R_{n}C_{L}$

with $R_{n,p}\approx 1/k_{n,p}(V_{DD}-V_{T})$ in triode.

Dynamic power :

$$P_{D}= P_{stat}+P_{sc}+P_{dyn}\approx C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f + V_{DD}I_{sc,av}$$

$P_{stat}\approx V_{DD}I_{leak}\to 0$ is the great advantage of CMOS.

Inverter is ratioless, can be scaled, fundamental cell for NAND, NOR, SRAM, ring oscillators and every CMOS digital IC. Equal sized $W_{p}\approx 2-3\,W_{n}$ gives symmetric rise/fall times.

answer.text:
This is the fundamental CMOS logic building
block - the {\it Complementary MOS Inverter} or {\it NOT Gate}
and at the same time a {\it class A push-pull inverting amplifier}.

$$M_{1}: NMOS\;\; ,S=GND \;\; V_{BS1}=0$$
$$M_{2}: PMOS\;\; ,S=V_{DD} \;\; V_{BS2}=0$$

no body effect if $n-$ well/$p-$ substrate is tied to the
source. Common gate input $V_{in}$, common drain output $V_{out}$.

It is {\it ratio-less}, {\it rail to rail} logic with ideally
{\it zero static power}.

### 1. Principle of operation

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}\;\;{\rm in\;d.c.\;steady\;state}$$

For a long channel, neglect $\lambda$ for first order:

$$I_{Dn}=k_{n}(V_{GSn}-V_{Tn})^{2}/2\;\; {\rm sat.}$$
$$k_{n}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}\;\;,k_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$$
$$I_{Dp}=k_{p}(V_{SGp}+V_{Tp})^{2}/2\;\; {\rm sat.}\;\;V_{Tp}<0$$

* $V_{in}=0 = V_{OL}<V_{Tn}$:

$V_{GS1}=0<V_{Tn}\to M_{1}$ {\bf OFF}, $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{Tp}|\to M_{2}$ {\bf ON}
No DC path to GND. $M_{2}$ charges the output capacitance to $V_{DD}$ through its low $R_{on}$, in steady state $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $I_{DD}=0$ ( leakage only). $M_{2}$ is in triode/linear because $V_{SD2}=0< V_{SG2}+V_{Tp}$.

* $V_{in}=V_{DD}=V_{OH}>V_{Tn}$:

$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{Tn}\to M_{1}$ {\bf ON}, $V_{SG2}=0<|V_{Tp}|\to M_{2}$ {\bf OFF}
No DC path to $V_{DD}$. $M_{1}$ discharges the load to $GND$, $V_{OL}=0$, $I_{DD}=0$. $M_{1}$ is in triode.

In words: Pull-up network ($M_{2}$) and pull-down network ($M_{1}$) are never ON simultaneously in steady state. Logic function:

$$V_{out} = \bar V_{in}$$

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ NMOS | $M_{2}$ PMOS | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ | OFF | Linear | $V_{DD}$ |
| $L$ | OFF/Sat | Linear | $\approx V_{DD}$ |
| $V_{M}$ | Sat | Sat | $V_{M}\approx V_{DD}/2$ |
| $H$ | Linear | Sat/OFF | $\approx 0$ |
| $V_{DD}$ | Linear | OFF | $0$ |

### 2. Voltage Transfer Characteristic - VTC

Five regions for increasing $V_{in}$ $0\to V_{DD}$:

1.  $M1$ off, $M2$ linear : $V_{out}=V_{DD}$
2.  $M1$ saturation, $M2$ linear
3.  $M1$ {\bf saturation}, $M2$ {\bf saturation} : High gain transition. Both saturated only for a narrow $V_{in}$ around the logic threshold.
4.  $M1$ linear, $M2$ saturation
5.  $M1$ linear, $M2$ off : $V_{out}=0$

Ideal VTC is very steep in region 3, approximating an ideal inverter.

The logic threshold or switching point $V_{M}$ defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$ where $I_{Dn}=|I_{Dp}|$ both in saturation:

$$\frac{k_{n}}{2}(V_{M}-V_{Tn})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{M}) = \frac{k_{p}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{M}+V_{Tp})^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}(V_{DD}-V_{M}))$$

For $\lambda\approx 0$:

$$V_{M}= \frac{V_{Tn}+ \sqrt{k_{p}/k_{n}}\,(V_{DD}+V_{Tp})}{1+\sqrt{k_{p}/k_{n}}}$$

If inverter is symmetric $k_{n}=k_{p}$, $V_{Tn}=|V_{Tp}|=V_{T}$:

$$V_{M}=V_{DD}/2$$

Noise margins are obtained from $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$ points $V_{IL},V_{IH}$:

$$NM_{L}=V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL}$$
$$NM_{H}=V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH}$$

For symmetric design $NM_{L}=NM_{H}\approx 0.4\,V_{DD}$, excellent noise immunity and full $0$ to $V_{DD}$ swing.

Current characteristic is a narrow peak at $V_{M}$ with
$I_{D,max}\approx k(V_{DD}/2-V_{T})^{2}/2$, zero elsewhere. Hence static power $P_{s}=V_{DD}I_{leak}\approx 0$.

### 3. Small signal - analog amplifier view

Biased at $V_{M}$ in region 3, both devices saturated, the circuit is a high gain push-pull common source amplifier.

Small signal model: Gates common, drains common.

$$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$$
$$g_{o}=g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}= \lambda_{n}I_{D}+ \lambda_{p}I_{D}$$
$$r_{o}=1/g_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$$A_{v}= \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} = -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

Typically $20$ to $>40\,dB$ with $r_{o}\sim 10k - 100k\Omega$, $g_{m}\sim 0.1-1\,mA/V$. Input resistance $\to \infty$, output resistance $r_{o}$.

Transition gain in large signal:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{1}{(V_{M}-V_{Tn})\lambda_{n}+ (V_{DD}-V_{M}+V_{Tp})\lambda_{p}}$$

Bandwidth limited by load capacitance $C_{L}$ at output node:

$$f_{-3dB}\approx 1/2\pi r_{o}C_{L}$$

Slew rate $SR = I_{D}/C_{L}$.

Dynamic power when switching at frequency $f$:

$$P_{D}= C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f + V_{DD}I_{sc}$$

where $I_{sc}$ is short circuit current during transition when both conduct, and propagation delay for a step input:

$$t_{pLH}\approx 0.69 R_{p}C_{L}\;\;,\;\;t_{pHL}\approx 0.69 R_{n}C_{L}$$
$$t_{p}= (t_{pLH}+t_{pHL})/2$$

with $R_{n,p}\approx 1/k_{n,p}(V_{DD}-V_{T})$.

> In digital application it is used as a NOT gate, buffer, and the basic element for NAND/NOR, SRAM, latch, ring oscillator. In analog it is the simplest CMOS operational transconductance inverter stage, often used as output stage or as a high gain stage with active load - essentially $M_{1}$ is the driver and $M_{2}$ is its active load and vice versa.

Ideal characteristics: full logic swing, regenerative VTC, high $NM$, zero static current, ratioless design - area and operation independent of transistor sizing ratio except for $V_{M}$ and speed.

This is the Complementary MOS, CMOS, NOT gate - {\bf Inverter} the basic building block of all static CMOS logic.

$$M_{1}= NMOS\; driver \;\; ; \;M_{2}= PMOS\; active\; load$$
$$M_{1}: V_{GS1}= V_{in} \;, \;V_{DS1}=V_{out}$$
$$M_{2}: V_{SG2}= V_{DD}-V_{in}\;, \; V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$

Bulk of $M_{1}$ to $GND$ and bulk of $M_{2}$ to $V_{DD}$ so for this connection $V_{SB}=0$ no body effect. Both are enhancement mode, $V_{Tn}>0 ,\;V_{Tp}<0$.

$$I_{Dn}= \begin{cases}
0 & V_{GS}<V_{Tn}\;\;cut-off\\
k_{n}\left[(V_{GS}-V_{Tn})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^{2}/2\right] & V_{DS}<V_{GS}-V_{Tn}\;\;triode\\
\frac{k_{n}}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{Tn})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS}) & V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{Tn}\;\;saturation
\end{cases}$$

$$k_{n}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1} \quad , \quad k_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$$

and dual for $M_{2}$ with $V_{SG},V_{SD},|V_{Tp}|$.

In DC steady state $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$.

### 1. Logic Operation

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ NMOS | $M_{2}$ PMOS | $V_{out}$ | Logic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0 = GND$ | $V_{GS}<V_{Tn} \rightarrow OFF$ | $V_{SG}=V_{DD} >|V_{Tp}|\rightarrow ON$ | $V_{out}=V_{DD}$ through $M_{2}$ | $0 \rightarrow 1$ |
| $V_{DD}$ | $V_{GS}=V_{DD} \rightarrow ON$ | $V_{SG}=0 \rightarrow OFF$ | $V_{out}=0$ through $M_{1}$ | $1 \rightarrow 0$ |

Hence $V_{out}= \bar V_{in}$ . In static state one transistor is always OFF so ideal {\it static current $=0$} and static power $P_{stat}\approx 0$.

$$V_{OH}=V_{DD} \quad , \quad V_{OL}=0$$

Full rail to rail swing - ratioless logic.

### 2. Voltage Transfer Characteristic - 5 Regions

With $V_{in}$ swept $0 \to V_{DD}$:

* {\bf A: $0 \le V_{in} < V_{Tn}$} 
  $M_{1}$ OFF, $M_{2}$ triode. $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

* {\bf B: $V_{Tn} < V_{in} < V_{in,1}$}
  $M_{1}$ saturation, $M_{2}$ triode.

* {\bf C: $V_{in} \approx V_{M}$} 
  Both saturation. Very high gain region. This is the switching threshold where $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$.

  Ignoring $\lambda$:
  $$\frac{k_{n}}{2}(V_{M}-V_{Tn})^{2}= \frac{k_{p}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{M}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}$$

  $$V_{M}= \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|+ \sqrt{k_{n}/k_{p}}\;V_{Tn}}{1+\sqrt{k_{n}/k_{p}}}= \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|+ \sqrt{\beta_{R}}V_{Tn}}{1+\sqrt{\beta_{R}}}$$

  with $\beta_{R}=k_{n}/k_{p}$. For matched device $k_{n}=k_{p}$ and $V_{Tn}=|V_{Tp}|=V_{T}$:

  $$V_{M}=V_{DD}/2$$

  Commonly $(W/L)_{p} \approx 2-3 (W/L)_{n}$ to compensate $\mu_{n}\approx 2-3\mu_{p}$ and get symmetric $V_{M}$.

* {\bf D: $V_{in,2} < V_{in} < V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$}
  $M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ saturation.

* {\bf E: $V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}| < V_{in} \le V_{DD}$}
  $M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ OFF. $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

> VTC is a sharp inverted S. Slope $dV_{out}/dV_{in} \approx 0$ in regions A and E, slope $<<-1$ in C.

```
Vout
VDD |******
    |      *
    |       *
    |        *
    |         *
    |          *******
    +------------------ Vin
    0   VIL VM VIH  VDD
```

Noise margins defined by $|dV_{out}/dV_{in}|=1$:

$$N_{M_{L}} = V_{IL}-V_{OL} \quad , \quad N_{M_{H}} = V_{OH}-V_{IH}$$

For ideal symmetric inverter $N_{M_{L}} \approx N_{M_{H}} \approx 0.4\,V_{DD}$ - maximum.

### 3. Analog Small Signal Behaviour

If biased at $V_{in}=V_{M}$ region C both devices in saturation it is a high gain push-pull common source amplifier. Loaded by $C_{L}$:

$$A_{v} = \left.\frac{dV_{out}}{dV_{in}}\right|_{V_{M}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{r_{o1}^{-1}+r_{o2}^{-1}}$$

$$g_{m}=k(V_{GS}-V_{T})\;\;,\;\; r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}$$

Typically $|A_{v}| = 20$ to $100$ for long channel, $>10$ for short channel. This is why the transition is so sharp.

### 4. Dynamic Behaviour

No DC path, current only flows during switching when both transistors briefly conduct, short circuit current spike + charging/discharging $C_{L}$.

$$P_{dyn}= C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f + V_{DD}I_{sc} + P_{leak}$$

Propagation delay for $C_{L}$ load approx:

$$t_{pLH} \approx \frac{C_{L}V_{DD}}{2I_{Dp,sat}} \quad , \quad t_{pHL} \approx \frac{C_{L}V_{DD}}{2I_{Dn,sat}}$$

$$t_{p}= \frac{t_{pLH}+t_{pHL}}{2}$$

Designed for $t_{pLH}=t_{pHL}$ via $k_{n}=k_{p}$ sizing.

In short: As {\bf digital gate} it is an ideal inverter with near zero static power, full logic swing and regenerative VTC. As {\bf analog circuit} at $V_{M}$ it is a high gain inverting amplifier.

If you give $V_{DD}, V_{Tn}, |V_{Tp}|, (W/L)_{1,2}, k_{n}',k_{p}'$ the $V_{M}, V_{IL},V_{IH}$, gain and $t_{p}$ can be calculated numerically.

This is the static CMOS logic inverter.

$M_1$ is the NMOS pull-down, $M_2$ is the PMOS pull-up.
Assume bulk to source: $V_{SB1}=0$, $V_{SB2}=0$.

$$k_n=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1 \;\;,\;\; k_p=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2$$
$$V_{TN}>0 \;\;,\;\; V_{TP}=-|V_{TP}|<0$$

$$I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2(1+\lambda_nV_{DS})$$
in saturation, $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{TN}$

$$I_{Dn} = k_n\left[(V_{GS}-V_{TN})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2\right]$$
in triode.

PMOS with $V_{SG}, V_{SD}, |V_{TP}|$ dual.

$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$.

Saturation conditions:

NMOS: $V_{out} \ge V_{in}-V_{TN}$ sat, else linear
PMOS: $V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{in}+V_{TP}$ sat, i.e.
$$V_{out} \le V_{in}-V_{TP}$$
else linear. Since $V_{TP}<0$, the window
$$V_{in}-V_{TN} \le V_{out} \le V_{in}-V_{TP}$$
is where both can saturate.

### 1. Logic operation

$V_{in}=0$ low:
$$V_{GS1}=0<V_{TN} : M_1\; OFF$$
$$V_{GS2}=-V_{DD}<V_{TP} : M_2\; ON$$
Output is pulled via $M_2$ to $V_{DD}$. $V_{SD2}\approx 0$,
$M_2$ deep triode.

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ high:
$$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN} : M_1\; ON$$
$$V_{SG2}=0<|V_{TP}| : M_2\; OFF$$
Output is pulled via $M_1$ to $0$. $M_1$ deep triode.

Hence
$$V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$$
with full rail:
$$V_{OL}\approx 0,\;V_{OH}\approx V_{DD}$$

In a stable state one device is OFF, so ideally
static $I_{DD}=0$. Static power is only leakage.

For $V_{in}$ swept $0\to V_{DD}$:

1. Region 1: $0\le V_{in}<V_{TN}$ : $M_1$ off, $M_2$ linear. $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. Region 2: $M_1$ sat, $M_2$ linear. $V_{out}$ falls from $V_{DD}$.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 = k_p\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\right]$$

3. Region 3: $M_1$ sat, $M_2$ sat. Narrow high gain region.
$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2(1+\lambda_nV_{out})=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2(1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{out}))$$

4. Region 4: $M_1$ linear, $M_2$ sat.
$$k_n\left[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right]=\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2$$

5. Region 5: $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ : $M_1$ linear, $M_2$ off. $V_{out}=0$.

This gives the classic sharp voltage transfer characteristic, VTC.

### 2. Switching threshold

$V_M$ defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$. At that point
both are almost certainly in saturation. Neglecting $\lambda$:

$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{TN})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

$$\sqrt{\frac{k_n}{k_p}}(V_M-V_{TN}) = V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|$$

Let $r=\sqrt{k_n/k_p}$. Then

$$V_M = \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|+r\,V_{TN}}{r+1}$$

In particular if $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|=V_T$ and $k_n=k_p$,
$$V_M=V_{DD}/2$$
Stronger NMOS, larger $k_n$, moves $V_M$ down toward $V_{TN}$.
Stronger PMOS moves $V_M$ up toward $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$.
Since $\mu_n\approx 2$-$3\,\mu_p$, symmetric threshold
requires $(W/L)_p\approx 2$-$3\,(W/L)_n$.

### 3. Small signal in transition

In region 3 both act as common-source, one as load of
the other. Gates common to $v_{in}$, drains common to $v_{out}$,
sources ac ground.

KCL at output gives:

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{out}+g_{m2}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}=0$$

$$A_v =\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$
$$= -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}||r_{o2})$$

with at bias $I_D$:

$$g_m = \sqrt{2kI_D}= \frac{2I_D}{V_{GS}-V_T}$$
$$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_n I_D,\; r_{o2}=1/\lambda_p I_D$$

$|A_v|$ is large, typically 20-50. Hence the VTC is almost
vertical in region 3.

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}||r_{o2},\;\; R_{in}=\infty$$

Biased at $V_M$, e.g. with resistive feedback, it is a
high gain analog inverting amplifier.

$V_{IL}, V_{IH}$ are defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$
in regions 2 and 4. Noise margins:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL},\; NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}$$

approx $V_{DD}/2$ for symmetric high-gain design.

### 4. Power and speed

No static current except during transition where both
conduct briefly: short-circuit current.

Dynamic power to charge load $C_L$ at frequency $f$:

$$P_{dyn}= \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

Propagation delay set by current drive in saturation/triode
charging $C_L$:

$t_{pHL}$: $M_1$ discharging, $t_{pLH}$: $M_2$ charging.
Approximately $0.69 R_{eq}C_L$.

In sum: rail-to-rail inverting gate, zero nominal static power,
high noise margin, high gain in threshold region, the
fundamental CMOS gate.

answer.text:
This is a static CMOS inverter. The fundamental
CMOS gate.

* $M_{1}$ : NMOS pull down. source to $GND$.
$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$
* $M_{2}$ : PMOS pull up. source to $V_{DD}$.
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$
with $V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{DD}$

Bulk is tied to source: $M_{1}$ body to $GND$,
$M_{2}$ n-well to $V_{DD}$. No body effect.

Let

$$ k_{n} = \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}, \quad k_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2} $$
$$ I_{Dn} = \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{GS1}-V_{THN})^{2}(1+\lambda_n V_{DS1}) $$
in saturation, $V_{DS} \ge V_{GS}-V_{THN}$,
$$ I_{Dp} = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_p V_{SD2}) $$
in saturation, $V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$.

In steady state $I_{Dn}=I_{Dp}$ because gates draw no DC
current. That defines $V_{out}$ vs $V_{in}$.

### 1. Logic operation

$M_{1}$ is OFF for $V_{GS1}<V_{THN}$, i.e.

$$ V_{in} < V_{THN} $$

$M_{2}$ is OFF for $V_{SG2}<|V_{THP}|$, i.e.

$$ V_{DD}-V_{in}<|V_{THP}| $$
$$ V_{in} > V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| $$

Hence:

* $V_{in}=0$ = Low: $M_1$ OFF, $M_2$ ON. No DC path
to $GND$. Output is pulled to $V_{DD}$ through $M_2$.
$$ V_{OH} \approx V_{DD} $$

* $V_{in}=V_{DD}$ = High: $M_2$ OFF, $M_1$ ON. No DC path
to $V_{DD}$. Output is pulled to $GND$ through $M_1$.
$$ V_{OL} \approx 0 $$

This is a NOT gate with rail-to-rail swing and,
ideally, zero static current in the two logic states.
One transistor is always OFF.

There is push-pull drive in both directions, so
low static output impedance.

### 2. Voltage transfer characteristic

Ignoring $\lambda$ for the shape, we have 5 regions.

I. $0 \le V_{in} < V_{THN}$:
$M_1$ OFF, $M_2$ in linear. $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

II. $V_{THN} \le V_{in} < V_M$:
$M_1$ saturation, $M_2$ triode.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{THN})^2 = 
\frac{k_p}{2}\left[2(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{THP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})-(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2\right] $$
$V_{out}$ falls fast from $V_{DD}$.

$V_M$ is the switching threshold where $V_{in}=V_{out}$.

III. $V_{in}\approx V_M$:
Both saturation.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{THN})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

IV. $V_M < V_{in} \le V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|$:
$M_1$ triode, $M_2$ saturation.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}\left[2(V_{in}-V_{THN})V_{out}-V_{out}^2\right]=\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{THP}|)^2 $$

V. $V_{DD}-|V_{THP}| < V_{in} \le V_{DD}$:
$M_2$ OFF, $M_1$ linear. $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

Boundary II-III: $M_2$ enters saturation:
$V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}-|V_{THP}|$, i.e. $V_{out}=V_{in}+|V_{THP}|$.
Boundary III-IV: $M_1$ enters saturation:
$V_{DS1}=V_{GS1}-V_{THN}$, i.e. $V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{THN}$.

With $\lambda=0$, region III is a vertical line with
infinite gain. With $\lambda_n,\lambda_p>0$ it has a
finite steep slope.

### 3. Switching threshold $V_M$

Put $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$ and $I_{Dn}=I_{Dp}$:

$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_M-V_{THN})^2(1+\lambda_n V_M)=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|)^2(1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_M)) $$

For $\lambda\approx 0$:

$$ \sqrt{k_n}\,(V_M-V_{THN}) = \sqrt{k_p}\,(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|) $$

$$ V_M = \frac{V_{THN}+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|)}{1+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}} $$

$V_M$ is set by ratio $k_p/k_n$, i.e. by sizing.

For symmetric $V_{THN}=|V_{THP}|=V_T$ and $V_M=V_{DD}/2$:

$$ \sqrt{\frac{k_p}{k_n}} = \frac{V_{DD}/2-V_{THN}}{V_{DD}/2-|V_{THP}|} $$

Ideally $k_n\approx k_p$. Since $\mu_n \approx 2\text{-}3\,\mu_p$,
this requires

$$ (W/L)_p \approx 2\text{-}3\,(W/L)_n .$$

Then PMOS is wider to compensate for lower hole mobility,
giving symmetric rise/fall.

### 4. Small-signal gain at $V_M$

At $V_M$ both devices are in saturation, common source,
gates common, drains common.

$$ g_{m1}=k_n(V_M-V_{THN}), \quad g_{m2}=k_p(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{THP}|) $$
$$ r_{o1}=1/(\lambda_n I_D), \quad r_{o2}=1/(\lambda_p I_D) $$

Small signal:

$$ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} = -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

Typically $-20$ to $-100$. This is why a CMOS inverter
biased at $V_M$, e.g. with resistive feedback from output
to input, is a high gain inverting amplifier.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$ are defined by $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$,
at the edges of the steep transition, in regions II and IV.
Noise margins:

$$ NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL} $$
$$ NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH} $$

For a symmetric inverter they are close to $V_{DD}/2$,
very large. E.g. with matched $k_n=k_p$, $V_{THN}=|V_{THP}|=V_T$:

$$ V_{IL}=\frac{3V_{DD}+2V_T}{8},\quad V_{IH}=\frac{5V_{DD}-2V_T}{8} $$

### 5. Dynamic and power

In static states $I_{DD}\approx 0$ except leakage.
Current flows only during transition, when both
transistors are momentarily ON - the crowbar / short-circuit
current, maximum near $V_M$.

With a load capacitance $C_L$, the delay is set by
charging/discharging $C_L$ through the saturation current
of $M_2$/$M_1$.

Roughly $t_{p} \propto C_L V_{DD}/I_{D,sat}$.
Symmetric $t_{pLH}\approx t_{pHL}$ if $k_n\approx k_p$.

Dynamic power for activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$:

$$ P_{dyn} = \alpha C_L V_{DD}^{2} f $$

plus short-circuit power during finite input rise/fall.

In summary: rail-to-rail inverting logic, high noise immunity,
essentially zero static power, active pull-up and pull-down,
and very high small-signal gain in the transition region.
That is why it is the core CMOS building block.

This is the static CMOS inverter. The logic NOT gate.

* $M_1$ bottom: NMOS, source to GND, drain to $V_{out}$
* $M_2$ top: PMOS, source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$

Both gates to $V_{in}$. Bodies to their sources,
NMOS body = p-sub = GND, PMOS body = n-well = $V_{DD}$,
so $V_{SB}=0$, no body effect.

Let for long channel square law

NMOS: $V_{TN}>0$, $k_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1$
PMOS: $V_{TP}<0$, $|V_{TP}|=-V_{TP}$,
$k_p = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_2$,
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}$, $V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$,
$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$.

Assume $V_{DD} > V_{TN}+|V_{TP}|$.

### 1. Ideal digital operation

MOS is a switch: NMOS on for gate high, PMOS on
for gate low.

$V_{in}=0$ low:
$V_{GS1}=0 < V_{TN}$: $M_1$ OFF
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{TP}|$: $M_2$ ON
Output pulled to $V_{DD}$ through $M_2$. No DC path
to GND because $M_1$ is off.

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ high:
$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN}$: $M_1$ ON
$V_{SG2}=0 < |V_{TP}|$: $M_2$ OFF
Output pulled to 0 through $M_1$. No DC path
to $V_{DD}$ because $M_2$ is off.

Hence:

```
Vin = 0   -> Vout = VDD
Vin = VDD -> Vout = 0
```

Inverter with rail-to-rail swing, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$,
$V_{OL}=0$, infinite DC input impedance, zero
static supply current except leakage.

During transition both devices are momentarily on,
giving a crowbar current from $V_{DD}$ to GND.

### 2. Voltage transfer characteristic

Equate $I_{DN}=|I_{DP}|$. Neglect $\lambda$ for DC levels.

I. $V_{in}<V_{TN}$:
$M_1$ cut-off, $M_2$ linear with $V_{SD}\approx 0$.
$V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $I_D=0$.

II. $V_{TN}<V_{in}<V_M$:
$M_1$ saturated, $M_2$ linear.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 =
k_p\Big[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^2}{2}\Big] $$
$V_{out}$ falls from $V_{DD}$.

III. $V_{in}\approx V_M$:
Both saturated. High gain.
$$ \frac{k_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TN})^2 =
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

IV. $V_M<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$:
$M_1$ linear, $M_2$ saturated.
$$ k_n\Big[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\Big]=
\frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)^2 $$

V. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$:
$M_2$ cut-off, $M_1$ linear with $V_{DS}\approx 0$.
$V_{out}=0$, $I_D=0$.

That gives the familiar sharp VTC with flat top
and bottom and steep transition. With $\lambda>0$
region III has finite negative slope, regions I,V
are still flat because current is zero.

### 3. Switching threshold $V_M$

Defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$, both in
saturation. Ignoring $\lambda$:

$$\sqrt{k_n}(V_M-V_{TN})=\sqrt{k_p}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)$$

$$V_M = \frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)}
{1+\sqrt{k_p/k_n}} $$

This is set by threshold and $\beta$-ratio.
If $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|=V_T$ and $k_n=k_p$:

$$V_M = V_{DD}/2$$

For equal strength $k_n=k_p$ we need:

$$\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}=\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}\approx 2-3$$

because PMOS mobility is lower.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$, the points where
$dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$, lie in regions II and IV.
Solving the current equation together with slope $=-1$
gives $V_{IL}<V_M<V_{IH}$ symmetrically around $V_M$
in the matched case. Noise margins are:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL}$$
$$NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{IH}\approx V_{DD}-V_{IH}$$

Close to $V_{DD}/2$ for a well sized inverter.

### 4. Small signal as amplifier

Biased at $V_M$, both devices are on in saturation,
forming a push-pull common-source amplifier.

$$A_v = -\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
= -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

with

$$g_{m1}=k_n(V_M-V_{TN}),\quad
g_{m2}=k_p(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{TP}|)$$
$$r_{o1}=1/\lambda_n I_D,\quad r_{o2}=1/\lambda_p I_D$$

Typically $|A_v|\sim 20-50$. Output resistance
in transition is $r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, large.
In logic 0 or 1 state, output resistance is the
linear-region $1/[k(V_{GS}-V_T)]$ of the ON device,
low.

Input capacitance is essentially the two gate
capacitances with Miller multiplication in the
transition region.

### 5. Dynamics and power

With load $C_L$, switching charges/discharges $C_L$
through $M_2$, $M_1$.

No static power: $P_{static}\approx 0$.

Dynamic power for activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$:

$$P_{dyn} = \alpha C_L V_{DD}^2 f$$

plus short-circuit power during the time both
transistors conduct.

Propagation delay $\approx R_{eq}C_L$. Rise time
set by PMOS strength, fall time by NMOS strength.
Equal $t_{pLH}\approx t_{pHL}$ requires
$k_n\approx k_p$, i.e. wider PMOS.

In short: rail-to-rail inverter, zero static
current, large noise margin, high gain in transition,
load-dependent speed and $CV_{DD}^2$ dynamic power.

The circuit is the static CMOS inverter, a NOT gate.

$M_{1}$ is the NMOS pull-down device, its source and body
to ground. $M_{2}$ is the PMOS pull-up device, its source and
body to $V_{DD}$. Hence there is no body effect. The gates
are the common input, the drains the common output.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{in}, & V_{DS1}&=V_{out}\\
V_{SG2}&=V_{DD}-V_{in}, & V_{SD2}&=V_{DD}-V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

Put 
$\beta_{n}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}$, $\beta_{p}=\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$,
$V_{tn}>0$, $V_{tp}<0$.

### Static operation

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ | $M_{2}$ | $V_{out}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $0$, logic 0 | OFF | ON | $V_{DD}$, logic 1 |
| $V_{DD}$, logic 1 | ON | OFF | $0$, logic 0 |

In either steady state one device is off, so (apart from
leakage) there is no d-c path $V_{DD}\to$ GND and no
static power. The output swings rail to rail,
$V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

With no d-c load $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. As $V_{in}$ rises from 0 to
$V_{DD}$, $V_{out}$ falls monotonically from $V_{DD}$ to 0.

1. $V_{in}<V_{tn}$: $M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ in triode with
$I_D=0$, so $V_{SD2}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. $V_{in}$ just $>V_{tn}$, $V_{out}$ still high: $M_{1}$
saturated, $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{tn}$; $M_{2}$ in triode,
$V_{out}>V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$.
$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{tn})^{2}
 =\beta_p\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
 -\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}}{2}\right]$$
$V_{out}$ falls slowly.

3. Intermediate $V_{in}$: both saturated,
$V_{in}-V_{tn}\le V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$. $V_{out}$
falls very rapidly, and a substantial "crowbar" current
flows from $V_{DD}$ to ground.

4. $V_{in}$ large, $V_{out}$ low: $M_{1}$ in triode, $M_{2}$
saturated, the mirror image of 2.

5. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$: $M_{2}$ off, $M_{1}$ in triode
with $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

```
Vout
VDD |------\
    |       \
    |        \     <- very steep, both saturated
  0 |         ------
    +-------------- Vin
              VM
```

### Switching threshold

Define $V_M$ by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$. Both devices are in
saturation there, so, neglecting $\lambda$,
$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_M-V_{tn})^2=
 \frac{\beta_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{tp}|)^2$$
$$\;V_M=
\frac{V_{tn}+r\,(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)}{1+r}\;,
\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{\beta_p}{\beta_n}}$$

For $\beta_n=\beta_p$ and $V_{tn}=|V_{tp}|$, $V_M=V_{DD}/2$.
Since $\mu_n\approx 2$–$3\,\mu_p$, a symmetric inverter
normally makes $(W/L)_2\approx(\mu_n/\mu_p)(W/L)_1$, at
the cost of area and input capacitance.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$ are the $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$ points.
With $V_{OL}=0$, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$,
$NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL}$, $NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}$, both typically
$\sim 0.4V_{DD}$, i.e. excellent noise immunity.

Biased at $V_M$ the circuit is also a high-gain inverting
amplifier: both transistors act as common-source devices
in parallel,
$$A_v=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$
which explains the steep VTC. Finite $\lambda$ makes the
slope finite but large.

### Dynamic behaviour and power

The output sees a load capacitance $C_L$ (next gate,
parasitics, wiring). $M_{2}$ charges $C_L$ to $V_{DD}$,
$M_{1}$ discharges it to ground. To first order,
$$t_{pHL}\sim \frac{C_LV_{DD}}{\beta_n(V_{DD}-V_{tn})^2},
\qquad
t_{pLH}\sim \frac{C_LV_{DD}}{\beta_p(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)^2}$$
or $t_p\approx0.69R_{eq}C_L$. Equal rise and fall times
again require $\beta_n\approx\beta_p$.

Static power is $\approx V_{DD}I_{leak}$ only. On a
$0\to1$ output transition $C_LV_{DD}^{2}$ is drawn from
the supply, half dissipated in $M_{2}$, half stored on
$C_L$ and later dissipated in $M_{1}$. For activity
factor $\alpha$ and frequency $f$,
$$P_{dyn}= \alpha f C_L V_{DD}^{2}$$
plus a smaller short-circuit term from the interval in
region 3 when both devices conduct.

In summary: a complementary, rail-to-rail, inverting
stage with infinite d-c input resistance, low output
resistance, essentially zero static power, large noise
margins, and speed/power dominated by $C_LV_{DD}^{2}f$ —
the basic building block of static CMOS logic.

answer.text:
The circuit is the CMOS inverter. $M_{1}$ is an
NMOS device, its body tied to ground, its source to ground
and its drain to the output. $M_{2}$ is a PMOS device, its
body tied to $V_{DD}$, its source to $V_{DD}$ and its drain
to the output. The gates are tied together.

$$V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$$

Since the source of each device is tied to its body,
$V_{BS}=0$ for both devices and there is no body effect.

### Steady state operation

Let $V_{TN}>0$ be the NMOS threshold and $V_{TP}<0$
the PMOS threshold.

$V_{in}=0$:
$$V_{GS1}=0<V_{TN}\qquad V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{TP}|$$
$M_{1}$ is off, $M_{2}$ is on. There is no dc path from
$V_{DD}$ to ground, and $M_{2}$ pulls the output to

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}\qquad \text{logic 1}$$

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$:
$$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN}\qquad V_{SG2}=0<|V_{TP}|$$
$M_{2}$ is off, $M_{1}$ is on. $M_{1}$ pulls the output to

$$V_{out}=0\qquad \text{logic 0}$$

Hence the output swings rail-to-rail,
$V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$. In either steady state one
transistor is off, so ideally

$$I_{DD,static}=0,\qquad P_{static}\approx 0$$

except for leakage. The input draws no dc current,
the static output resistance is low, because the
on transistor is in the triode region with $V_{DS}\approx 0$.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

As $V_{in}$ is raised from $0$ to $V_{DD}$, five regions occur.

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ NMOS | $M_{2}$ PMOS | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $V_{in}<V_{TN}$ | off | triode | $V_{DD}$ |
| low | saturation | triode | $\approx V_{DD}$, falling slowly |
| $V_{in}\approx V_{M}$ | saturation | saturation | falls steeply |
| high | triode | saturation | $\approx 0$, falling slowly |
| $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ | triode | off | $0$ |

In the middle region both devices are saturated, so the
small signal voltage gain is large. With both gates driven
and both drains at the output,

$$A_{v}=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) ,\qquad |A_{v}|\gg 1$$

so the VTC is very steep around its switching point.

### Switching threshold

Define $V_{M}$ by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$. There both devices
are saturated and $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. Neglecting $\lambda$,

$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{M}-V_{TN})^{2}
 =\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{M}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}$$

where $\beta_{n,p}=\mu_{n,p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{n,p}$. Hence

$$V_{M}=
\frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\,\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)}
     {1+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}} .$$

If $\beta_n=\beta_p$ and $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|$,

$$V_{M}= \frac{V_{DD}}{2}$$

at the centre of the supply range. Since $\mu_n\approx 2$--$3\,\mu_p$,
this usually requires

$$\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_p \approx \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}
\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n $$

i.e. the PMOS is made wider than the NMOS. This also
equalises the rise and fall times.

Noise margins are defined from the points where
$dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$, $V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$:

$$NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL}=V_{IL},\qquad 
  NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}=V_{DD}-V_{IH}.$$

For a balanced inverter they are each close to $V_{DD}/2$,
so the inverter has excellent noise immunity and restores
logic levels at every stage.

### Switching, power and speed

During a transition, for $V_{TN}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$,
both transistors are on briefly, producing a short
``crowbar'' current from $V_{DD}$ to ground. This is the
main short-circuit power component.

With a load capacitance $C_L$ at the output, a $0\to1$
transition draws $C_LV_{DD}^{2}$ of energy from the supply,
half stored on $C_L$ and half dissipated in $M_{2}$; the
stored energy is dissipated in $M_{1}$ on the $1\to0$
transition. For switching activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$,

$$P_{dyn}\approx \alpha C_L V_{DD}^{2} f .$$

The propagation delays are approximately set by charging
$C_L$ through the on resistance of $M_{2}$ and discharging
it through $M_{1}$:

$$t_{PLH}\approx 0.69\,R_{eq,p}C_L,\qquad
  t_{PHL}\approx 0.69\,R_{eq,n}C_L,$$
$$t_p=\frac{t_{PLH}+t_{PHL}}{2}.$$

In summary, the circuit is a NOT gate with rail-to-rail
swing, very high input impedance, low static output
impedance, essentially zero static power, large noise
margins, and speed/power determined mainly by the load
capacitance and the transistor sizes.

\,V_M=

r=\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\;  .

answer.text:
The drawing is the elementary CMOS inverter – a complementary pair consisting of  

• M₂ : a p-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to the positive supply VDD  
• M₁ : an n-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to ground  

The two drains are shorted to form the output node Vout, and the two gates are shorted to the input node Vin.  
Only one device conducts in the static states, so the quiescent (dc) power loss is ideally zero.

1. Logic (qualitative) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V → M₁ off (VGSₙ < VTN), M₂ on (VSGₚ > |VTP|) → Vout pulled to VDD (logic 1).  
   b) Vin ≈ VDD → M₂ off (VSGₚ < |VTP|), M₁ on (VGSₙ > VTN) → Vout pulled to 0 V (logic 0).  
   Thus the stage performs the NOT function.

2. D-C transfer characteristic  
   Let βn = μnCox(W/L)n and βp = μpCox(W/L)p.  
   In the transition region (VTN < Vin < VDD – |VTP|) the two devices conduct simultaneously and, to first order, both are in saturation. Equating their drain currents

          βn/2 · (Vin – Vout – VTN)²  =  βp/2 · (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²        (1)

   gives Vout(Vin).  For the special case βn = βp and |VTP| = VTN the locus is

          Vout = 2Vin – VDD

   and the switching (mid-point) voltage, obtained by also requiring dVout/dVin = –1, is very close to VDD/2.  With unequal β–values the switching point is

          VM ≈ (VDD + |VTP| + √(βp/βn)·VTN) / (1 + √(βp/βn))

   which is centred by choosing (W/L)p ≈ (μn/μp)(W/L)n so that βp ≈ βn.

3. Noise margins  
   VIL and VIH are obtained from |dVout/dVin| = 1 in (1); the noise margins follow

          NML = VIL – VOL     ,     NMH = VOH – VIH
          VOL ≈ 0 , VOH ≈ VDD

   Because the gain |dVout/dVin| in the transition region can exceed 40–50, good noise margins (typically > 0.4 VDD) are obtained.

4. Dynamic behaviour  
   • Low-to-high delay (n-device releases load):

          tPLH ≈ Rp · CL ≈ CL / [βp (VDD – |VTP|)]                        

   • High-to-low delay (n-device pulls down):

          tPHL ≈ Rn · CL ≈ CL / [βn (VDD – VTN)]

   Matching βp to βn equalises the two delays.  
   Dynamic power: Pdyn = CL VDD² fCLK ; short-circuit power exists only for the brief time both devices conduct.

5. Key features that make the CMOS inverter the basic building block of modern digital ICs  
   • Rail-to-rail output swing (0 – VDD)  
   • Large noise margins determined mainly by device sizing, not by resistor ratios  
   • Essentially zero static power (only leakage)  
   • Symmetric transfer when βp ≈ βn, giving equal rise/fall delays  
   • Very high input resistance; fan-out determined by capacitive loading only

Hence the circuit in the figure is a standard complementary MOS inverter and its behaviour is completely described by the relations above.

2. Static (DC) behaviour  
   a. Vin = 0 V (logic 0)  
      – pMOS: VSG = VDD  ⇒ ON  
      – nMOS: VGS = 0     ⇒ OFF  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled up to VDD  (logic 1).

   b. Vin = VDD (logic 1)  
      – pMOS: VSG ≈ 0     ⇒ OFF  
      – nMOS: VGS = VDD   ⇒ ON  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled down to 0 V  (logic 0).

   c. Intermediate Vin  
      Both transistors conduct simultaneously; the exact switching point VM is obtained from
            βn (Vin – Vtn)² = βp (VDD – Vin – |Vtp|)²
      (βn = kn Wn/Ln, βp = kp Wp/Lp).  
      If βn ≈ βp, VM ≈ VDD/2, giving nearly equal noise margins.

3. Voltage-transfer characteristic (VTC)  
   • VOL ≈ 0 V, VOH ≈ VDD (rail-to-rail).  
   • High small-signal gain (–dVout/dVin) around VM.  
   • Noise margins:  NML = VIL – VOL,  NMH = VOH – VIH; with symmetric sizing both approach VDD/2.

4. Dynamic operation  
   – Only one device conducts strongly while the other is OFF, so static power ≈ 0.  
   – During transitions both devices momentarily conduct, creating a short-circuit current but only for nanoseconds.  
   – Dynamic (switching) power:  Pdyn = CL VDD² fsw.  
   – Propagation delays (first-order):  
         tPHL ≈ 0.69 RN CL,  tPLH ≈ 0.69 RP CL,  
     where RN and RP are the equivalent on-resistances of the n- and p-devices.  
     Because μn ≈ 2–3 μp, designers make Wp ≈ 2–3 Wn to equalise tPHL and tPLH.

5. Summary of merits and drawbacks  
   + Rail-to-rail output swing  
   + Large noise margin  
   + Essentially zero static power  
   + Simple to cascade (output of one can directly drive the input of the next)  
   – Requires both n- and p-type devices (larger area than a single-device pull-up inverter).

• The two drains are shorted together and form the output node Vout.

     • PMOS: VSG-P = VDD > |Vthp| → ON, pulls Vout → VDD.  
     Result: Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”).  
   – Vin = VDD (logic “1”):  
     • PMOS: VSG-P = 0 < |Vthp| → OFF.  
     • NMOS: VGS-N = VDD > Vthn → ON, pulls Vout → 0.  
     Result: Vout ≈ 0 (logic “0”).  

   Hence the circuit inverts the input.

2. Regions of operation  
   • For Vin ≤ Vthn  → NMOS off, PMOS on (usually linear once Vout reaches VDD).  
   • For Vin ≥ VDD – |Vthp|  → PMOS off, NMOS on.  
   • For intermediate Vin both transistors conduct simultaneously; this is the only time a d.c. path exists between VDD and ground.

3. Static transfer characteristic  
   Ignoring channel-length modulation and using the square-law model,

     Idn = (βn/2)(Vin – Vthn)²  (saturation, since Vout ≈ Vin)  
     Idp = (βp/2)(VDD – Vin – |Vthp|)²

   At the switching point VM (Vin = Vout, Idn = Idp):

     (VM – Vthn)² / (VDD – VM – |Vthp|)² = βp / βn

     ⇒ VM = ( VDD + |Vthp| + √(βn/βp)·Vthn ) / (1 + √(βn/βp))

   With matched devices (βn ≈ βp, |Vthp| ≈ Vthn) the trip point is close to VDD/2, giving a symmetrical VTC and large noise margins.

4. Noise margins and logic levels  
   VOH ≈ VDD,  VOL ≈ 0  
   VIL and VIH are found where |dVout/dVin| = –1 on the VTC.  
   NMH = VOH – VIH,  NML = VIL – VOL  
   Because the gain around VM is large, NMH and NML are typically close to VDD/2.

5. Power  
   • Static power: essentially zero, because in either stable state one transistor is OFF, so no direct path exists from VDD to ground (leakage excepted).  
   • Dynamic power: Pd ≈ α·CL·VDD²·fclk + Pshort, where Pshort is the brief shoot-through current that flows while Vin is crossing the transition region.

6. Propagation delay (with load capacitance CL)  
   tpHL ≈ CL·(VDD – VM) / Idsn(Vin = VDD)  
   tpLH ≈ CL·VM / Idsp(Vin = 0)  
   With equal β’s the high-to-low and low-to-high delays are comparable.

Summary  
The circuit is the fundamental CMOS inverter:  
• Rail-to-rail output swing (0 → VDD).  
• Very small static power.  
• Large noise margins and steep transfer characteristic.  
• Propagation delays and switching threshold that can be tailored through the βn/βp ratio.

The circuit shown is a CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) inverter, also known as an inverting logic gate. It consists of two transistors: \( M_1 \), which is an n-channel MOSFET (NMOS), and \( M_2 \), which is a p-channel MOSFET (PMOS). The NMOS transistor \( M_1 \) is connected between the output node \( V_{\text{out}} \) and ground, while the PMOS transistor \( M_2 \) is connected between the output node \( V_{\text{out}} \) and the power supply \( V_{DD} \).

### Operation:

1. **When \( V_{\text{in}} \) is Low (0):**
   - The NMOS transistor \( M_1 \) is off because its gate-to-source voltage \( V_{GS1} \) is less than its threshold voltage \( V_{TN} \).
   - The PMOS transistor \( M_2 \) is on because its gate-to-source voltage \( V_{GS2} \) is negative and greater in magnitude than its threshold voltage \( |V_{TP}| \).
   - Since \( M_2 \) is on, it connects \( V_{\text{out}} \) to \( V_{DD} \), making \( V_{\text{out}} \) high (1).

2. **When \( V_{\text{in}} \) is High (1):**
   - The NMOS transistor \( M_1 \) is on because its gate-to-source voltage \( V_{GS1} \) is greater than its threshold voltage \( V_{TN} \).
   - The PMOS transistor \( M_2 \) is off because its gate-to-source voltage \( V_{GS2} \) is positive and less than its threshold voltage \( |V_{TP}| \).
   - Since \( M_1 \) is on, it connects \( V_{\text{out}} \) to ground, making \( V_{\text{out}} \) low (0).

### Characteristics:
- **Inversion:** The output \( V_{\text{out}} \) is the logical inverse of the input \( V_{\text{in}} \). If \( V_{\text{in}} \) is high, \( V_{\text{out}} \) is low, and vice versa.
- **Low Power Consumption:** When the input is stable (either high or low), only one of the transistors is conducting, minimizing static power consumption.
- **High Noise Immunity:** The CMOS inverter has good noise immunity due to the large separation between the high and low output levels.

This type of circuit is widely used in digital electronics for implementing logic functions and signal inversion.

## Circuit identification

The schematic is a **CMOS (complementary MOS) inverter** – the basic static‑logic gate.

| Node | Connection |
|------|------------|
| $V_{in}$ | Common **gate** of M1 (NMOS) and M2 (PMOS) |
| $V_{out}$ | Common **drain** of M1 and M2 |
| M1 source | Ground (0 V) |
| M2 source | $V_{DD}$ |

The two transistors form a "pull‑down network" (NMOS to ground) in series with a "pull‑up network" (PMOS to $V_{DD}$), both controlled by the same input. Because the PMOS is the complement of the NMOS (one is ON whenever the other is OFF), the gate is *complementary*.

## DC operation (truth table)

| $V_{in}$ | $V_{GS1}$ (NMOS) | $V_{SG2}$ (PMOS) | M1 | M2 | $V_{out}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 (L) | $0 < V_{TN}$ | $V_{DD} > |V_{TP}|$ | OFF | ON | $V_{DD}$ (H) |
| $V_{DD}$ (H) | $V_{DD} > V_{TN}$ | $0 < |V_{TP}|$ | ON | OFF | 0 (L) |

So in the static (logic) region the gate performs **$V_{out} = \overline{V_{in}}$**, with a full rail‑to‑rail swing (0 → $V_{DD}$). This full swing is the key advantage over resistive‑load or depletion‑load inverters: the transistors act as near‑zero‑resistance switches, not as voltage dividers.

## Transfer characteristic $V_{out}(V_{in})$

- $0 \le V_{in} < V_{TN}$: M1 off, M2 on (linear region) → $V_{out} = V_{DD}$.
- $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}| < V_{in} \le V_{DD}$: M2 off, M1 on (linear region) → $V_{out} = 0$.
- Intermediate region: **both** devices conduct, usually in saturation. $V_{out}$ falls steeply from $V_{DD}$ to 0. This is the *transition* (or linear) region; its width $\Delta V = V_{in,H} - V_{in,L}$ decreases as the gain increases.

The small‑signal gain in the transition region (both saturated) is

$$A_v = -\frac{1}{\frac{1}{g_{m1}} + \frac{1}{g_{m2}}} \,(r_{ds1}\parallel r_{ds2}) \;\approx\; -g_m (r_{ds1}\parallel r_{ds2}) \ll 1 \text{ in magnitude (large gain)},$$

which is what makes the transition sharp.

**Switching (mid‑threshold) voltage $V_M$**, found by equating the two saturation currents when $V_{out}$ is such that both are saturated:

$$\tfrac{1}{2}k_n (V_M - V_{TN})^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}k_p (V_{DD} - V_M + V_{TP})^2$$

For a symmetric design ($k_n \approx k_p$, $|V_{TN}|=|V_{TP}|$) this gives $V_M \approx V_{DD}/2$.

## Noise margins

With $V_{M,H}$ and $V_{M,L}$ the input voltages at which gain = 1:

$$NM_L = V_{M,L} - V_{OL}, \qquad NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{M,H}$$

For a symmetric inverter, $NM_L \approx NM_H \approx (V_{DD} - V_M)/2$, which is large → high noise immunity.

## Power and signal properties

- **Static (DC) power ≈ 0.** In either logic state one transistor is OFF, so there is *no DC path* from $V_{DD}$ to ground (only sub‑threshold/gate leakage). This is the defining advantage of CMOS.
- **Dynamic power** occurs only during switching, when both devices are briefly ON and a short‑circuit (crowbar) current $I_{sc}$ flows from $V_{DD}$ to ground: $P_{dyn} \approx C_L V_{DD}^2 f + I_{sc} V_{DD} f$.
- **Input impedance ≈ ∞** (only the gate‑oxide capacitance $C_{gs}$); no DC input current.
- **No body effect:** NMOS source = bulk = 0 V, PMOS source = bulk = $V_{DD}$, so $V_{SB}=0$ for both and the thresholds are the nominal ones.
- **Output resistance** in each state is the ON resistance of the conducting device ($r_{on1}$ or $r_{on2}$); together they set the 3‑dB bandwidth $f_{-3dB} \approx 1/(2\pi (r_{ds1}\parallel r_{ds2}) C_L)$.

## Summary

The figure is the canonical **CMOS inverter**: an NMOS pull‑down (M1) and a PMOS pull‑up (M2) sharing a common gate ($V_{in}$) and a common drain ($V_{out}$). It inverts the input with a full 0‑to‑$V_{DD}$ swing, very high gain and steep transition, near‑zero static power dissipation, infinite input impedance, and wide noise margins – which is why it is the fundamental building block of essentially all modern digital and mixed‑signal integrated circuits.
